extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers querying literary agents, especially novelists (authors transitioning from YA to adult)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on querying literary agents and revising a novel (particularly an adult novel from an author known for YA), including query strategy, working with editors, and emotional/structural revision priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic query tracking and batching
rubrics_metrics.description: “I developed a system of sending out ten queries every couple of weeks. I kept fastidious notes on when I sent a query, the agent I queried, and the response (if there was one).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a disciplined querying schedule (batch queries) and detailed records of dates, agent names, and responses to monitor progress and avoid duplicate queries. Batching steady sends every few weeks helps maintain momentum and lets you measure response patterns over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize agents who represent similar books and are reputable
rubrics_metrics.description: “I started with agents who I most wanted to work with, ones who represented books that I thought were similar to mine in some ways, and agents who I’d heard were very good.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research agent lists and submission guidelines; open with top-fit agents whose lists match your book’s genre/tone. Prioritizing fit increases chances of interest; reputation matters for long-term career support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of agents' representation scope (they may require representing all your work)
rubrics_metrics.description: “While some agents do represent only adult work, I found that many of the agents I queried would only read my novel if they could represent all of my work.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether an agent will represent cross-genre/age-range work. If an agent requires representation of your entire output, that may limit who will read your manuscript and influence whether to change representation or adjust your submission list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect form rejections and varied personal feedback; extract instructive points
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of rejections: “Unfortunately, your project is not one that we think would be right for our agency at this time.” and “I think you are a good writer and you have a good idea. However, I wasn’t enthusiastic enough to move forward with representation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate canned form letters as well as more specific agent notes. Treat any specific critiques as data: catalogue recurring criticisms and use them to identify structural or voice problems rather than taking every rejection personally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use outside editorial help (developmental and line editing) when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: “I sought the help of independent editor Alexandra Shelley... She helped me find the focus of my story, the source of suspense and mystery in each chapter, and develop better characters. And she provided grueling line edits that included cutting dead wood, marking awkwardness in my prose, and cutting interior scenes that didn’t advance the plot.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring in an experienced editor to diagnose big-picture issues (focus, suspense, character development) and to perform rigorous line edits. Expect substantive suggestions: cut dead wood, remove scenes that don’t advance the plot, and flag awkward prose for reworking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise continuously while continuing to query
rubrics_metrics.description: “I continued to send out queries, too, even as my manuscript was in a constant state of flux. (Agents usually ask for the beginning chapters of a manuscript, and mine never changed that much.) With each edit, my book became more focused, and I found that more agents were providing individual feedback...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep submitting as you revise; iterative edits can improve responses. Note that opening chapters may remain relatively stable, so you can send partials while revising later sections. Use agent feedback to guide targeted revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on emotional resonance and a satisfying ending
rubrics_metrics.description: “Irene still wanted to see revisions to the ending and more emotional resonance in certain spots.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether scenes build emotional payoff and whether the ending resolves stakes and themes. Strengthen moments that should connect emotionally to readers; revise endings to increase clarity, closure, or emotional impact as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to change representation to align career/brand goals
rubrics_metrics.description: “So, I finally took the risk and parted ways with my children’s agent to pursue representation for all my work.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your current agent’s specialties conflict with your intended market (e.g., YA agent vs. adult fiction), consider finding an agent who will champion your whole career. Sometimes leaving a prior agent is necessary to secure the right fit for a new project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate persistence, flexibility, and creativity in revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Alexandra Shelley once told me, “It takes persistence, flexibility, and creativity to revise.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach revision as an iterative creative process: persist through setbacks, remain open to structural/voice changes, and apply creative problem-solving to fix plot or character issues rather than defending every original choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut dead wood, fix awkward prose, and remove scenes that don’t advance plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Editor provided “grueling line edits that included cutting dead wood, marking awkwardness in my prose, and cutting interior scenes that didn’t advance the plot.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rigorous line edits to trim excess description, eliminate repetitive or irrelevant scenes, tighten sentences, and ensure every scene serves character development or plot progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat individual agent feedback and phone conversations as opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: “With each edit, my book became more focused, and I found that more agents were providing individual feedback, with a few even phoning to chat.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agent offers personalized feedback or a phone call, prepare to discuss revisions, intentions, and publishing strategy. These interactions can yield useful guidance and may signal stronger interest than a standard rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalize high rejection rates and maintain hope
rubrics_metrics.description: “Kathryn Stockett received more than sixty rejections... Kate DiCamillo received more than four-hundred sixty rejections...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that many successful authors faced numerous rejections; use these anecdotes to reframe rejection as common rather than definitive. Sustained belief in your story supports continued revision and querying.
